title: Payment System
prompt: Design the system that lets our marketplace take card payments from buyers through an external payment provider and pay sellers later, without ever losing or double-counting money.

clarify.q: Do we process cards ourselves or use a payment provider (PSP)?
clarify.why: Using a PSP keeps raw card numbers out of our systems, which shrinks our compliance scope to almost nothing. It also means the PSP is a remote system we cannot share a transaction with.

clarify.q: Do we authorise and capture separately (charge when the order ships), or charge at once?
clarify.why: Separate capture adds a second PSP call and a state where money is reserved but not taken, which expires after some days.

clarify.q: Who do we pay out, and when?
clarify.why: Paying sellers means we hold their money for a while. That needs a ledger with balances per seller, not just a list of charges.

clarify.q: Which currencies, and do we convert?
clarify.why: Multiple currencies mean every amount carries its currency, and the ledger must never add amounts in different currencies.

clarify.q: Do we need refunds, partial refunds and chargebacks?
clarify.why: Each is a money movement that must hit the ledger and may arrive days later, often by webhook, not from our own request.

clarify.q: How many payments per day, and what is the peak?
clarify.why: The rate decides how we size PSP connections and whether one ledger database is enough.

clarify.q: Do we use more than one PSP?
clarify.why: Several PSPs add routing and failover, and reconciliation must run per provider.

functional: Buyers pay for an order with a card token from the PSP's hosted form; we never see raw card numbers.
Every payment request can be retried safely: one buyer action charges at most once.
Every money movement is recorded as balanced double-entry ledger lines.
Refunds and chargebacks are applied from our API or from PSP webhooks.
A daily job matches our records against the PSP's settlement report and flags every difference.
nonFunctional: Zero double charges and zero lost payments; money correctness beats availability.
Payment API p99 under 2 s including the PSP call; our own overhead under 150 ms.
99.95% availability for accepting payments; payouts can wait hours.
Ledger is append-only and every entry is traceable to a request, webhook or file line.
Reconciliation finishes within 6 hours of receiving the PSP's daily file.
outOfScope: Building our own card processing or holding card numbers.
Fraud scoring models (we call a risk service and use its answer).

assumptions: 10 M payments per day; peak hour 10× the average
Authorise and capture are separate: 2 PSP calls per payment
PSP call latency: p50 400 ms, slow tail about 2 s
About 4 ledger lines per payment on average (3 for the capture with its fee, plus refunds and payouts spread across payments) at ~200 bytes
Average payment $40; about 2 webhooks per payment

steps.label: PSP calls in flight at peak
steps.math: 1 160 × 2 calls ≈ 2 300 calls/s; × 2 s slow tail ≈ 4 600 open calls
steps.result: ≈ 4 600 concurrent outbound calls: async I/O and a large connection pool

steps.label: Ledger writes
steps.math: 10 M × 4 = 40 M lines/day; 40 M × 200 B = 8 GB/day

steps.label: Money at stake
steps.math: 10 M × $40 = $400 M/day; a 0.01% error rate = 1 000 payments, $40 k/day
steps.result: Even tiny error rates are real money, so reconciliation is not optional

estimates.takeaway: The throughput is modest; a sharded or well-sized Postgres handles 4,600 ledger inserts/s at peak. The hard part is correctness across a network boundary: thousands of in-flight PSP calls at peak means thousands of chances per second for a timeout where we do not know whether money moved. The design therefore leans on idempotency keys, a state machine per payment, an append-only ledger and daily reconciliation, rather than on raw speed.

api.note: Idempotency-Key header required. 'pending' means we are still finding out what the PSP did.
Idempotency-Key header. Partial capture allowed up to the authorised amount.
Idempotency-Key header. Sum of refunds cannot exceed the captured amount.
Clients poll this when they got 'pending'.
Verify the HMAC signature, store the raw event, answer fast; process asynchronously.

entities.name: Payment
fields: created | authorizing | authorized | capturing | captured | failed | refunded
entities.why: One row per buyer payment; the state machine lives here.

entities.name: PspAttempt
fields: sent to the PSP as its idempotency key
entities.why: Records exactly what we asked the PSP and what it said, including 'unknown' after a timeout.

entities.name: LedgerEntry
entities.why: The books. Debits equal credits per txnId; balances are sums. Never updated or deleted.

entities.name: Outbox / InboundEvent
fields: outgoing domain event or raw PSP webhook
entities.why: Outgoing events are published only after commit; incoming webhooks are stored once and processed idempotently.

data.note: Everything that must agree lives in one relational database, so a state change, its ledger lines and its outbox event commit together. Amounts are integers in minor units (cents) with a currency code. The ledger is append-only: a mistake is fixed by a new reversing entry, never by an UPDATE. At 10× scale I would shard by merchantId, keeping each payment and its ledger lines on the same shard, and keep platform-wide accounts (fees, PSP clearing) as per-shard sub-accounts that roll up.

hld.summary:
The checkout page loads the PSP's hosted card form, which returns a token; card numbers never touch us. The payment service receives the token with an idempotency key, creates the payment row, and runs a small state machine: record an attempt, call the PSP with the attempt id as the PSP's idempotency key, then write the result, the ledger lines and an outbox event in one transaction.

The PSP also tells us things on its own through webhooks (async approvals, chargebacks, settlements). A webhook receiver verifies the signature, stores the raw event once by its id and returns 200; a processor applies it through the same state machine. A relay publishes outbox events to the order and payout systems. Once a day a reconciler compares the PSP's settlement file with our ledger and opens a case for every mismatch.

diagram.title: Payment service, PSP and the ledger
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  B[Buyer checkout] --> API[Payment API]
  API --> PS[Payment service]
  PS --> DB[("Postgres payments and ledger")]
  PS --> PSP[External PSP]
  PSP -->|webhooks| WH[Webhook receiver]
  WH --> DB
  DB --> RL[Outbox relay]
  RL --> K[Event bus]
  K --> ORD[Order service]
  K --> PO[Payout service]
  PSP -->|daily settlement file| REC[Reconciler]
  REC --> DB
  REC --> OPS[Ops case queue]

flows.title: A buyer pays
steps: Client sends POST /payments with Idempotency-Key K.
Service inserts Payment(status created) with unique (merchant, K); a duplicate returns the stored result.
It inserts PspAttempt A (status sent) and commits, then calls the PSP authorise endpoint with idempotency key A.
On success, one transaction sets status authorized, records the response, writes balanced ledger lines and an outbox event.
The relay publishes PaymentAuthorized; the order service confirms the order.

flows.title: The PSP call times out
steps: After 10 s with no answer, the attempt is marked unknown and the API returns 202 pending.
A recovery worker retries the same call with the same key A; the PSP returns the original result instead of charging again.
If the PSP has no record of A, the worker marks the attempt failed and the payment can be retried with a new attempt.

flows.title: A chargeback arrives days later
steps: PSP posts a dispute webhook; the receiver verifies the HMAC and inserts it with dedupKey = PSP event id.
The processor moves the payment to disputed and writes ledger lines moving the amount from the seller's balance to a disputes account.
An outbox event tells the payout service to hold that amount from the next seller payout.

deepDives.title: Idempotency from the button to the PSP
deepDives.problem: A retry can happen at every hop: the buyer double-taps, the mobile app retries after a dropped connection, our service retries a PSP timeout. Each layer needs its own key, and the keys must chain so that one buyer action becomes at most one charge.

options.name: Key only at our API
options.how: Client sends an Idempotency-Key; we dedupe requests to /payments; PSP calls are retried without a key.
cons: A retried PSP call after a timeout can charge twice
Protects only half the path

options.name: Chained keys with stored attempts
options.how: Client key dedupes the payment row. Each PSP call gets its own attemptId, saved before the call and sent as the PSP's idempotency key. Retries of the same step reuse the same attemptId.
pros: Every hop is safe to retry
After a crash, the saved attempt tells us what we might have done
cons: More rows and states to manage
Relies on the PSP honouring idempotency keys for at least as long as we retry

options.name: Query before retry
options.how: On timeout, look up the charge at the PSP by our order id before deciding to retry.
pros: Works with PSPs that have weak idempotency support
cons: Lookups can lag behind the charge itself
Still racy if the first call lands after the lookup

deepDives.choice: Use chained keys with stored attempts, and add the PSP lookup as the fallback for attempts that stay unknown beyond the PSP's key retention window. The rule is: write the intent before the side effect, and make the side effect keyed by that intent. The client key is stored with a hash of the request, so reusing a key with a different amount returns 422 instead of silently returning an old answer.

diagram.title: A timeout that does not double-charge
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S as Payment service
  participant D as Database
  participant P as PSP
  C->>S: POST payments, key K
  S->>D: insert payment and attempt A
  S->>P: authorise, key A
  P--xS: timeout
  S->>D: mark attempt A unknown
  S-->>C: 202 pending
  S->>P: retry authorise, key A
  P-->>S: original result, approved
  S->>D: authorised, ledger lines, outbox
  C->>S: GET payment
  S-->>C: authorised

deepDives.title: A double-entry ledger
deepDives.problem: A single 'balance' column per seller gets updated by charges, fees, refunds and chargebacks from many places. When it drifts, nobody can tell why. We need a record that explains every cent and can be checked mechanically.

options.name: Mutable balance columns
options.how: UPDATE seller SET balance = balance + amount on each event.
cons: No history of why the balance is what it is
One lost or doubled update is invisible

options.name: Append-only double-entry lines
options.how: Every movement writes at least two lines in one transaction: debits equal credits per txnId. Balances are sums over an account, cached in a balance table updated in the same transaction.
pros: The books must balance, which catches bugs immediately
cons: More rows (about 4 per payment here)
Cached balances need periodic checking against the sums

deepDives.choice: Use append-only double entry. A $40 capture with a $1.20 fee writes: debit psp_clearing 4000, credit seller:42 3880, credit fees 120. Debits (4000) equal credits (3880 + 120). Each line carries a unique sourceRef, so replaying the same webhook cannot post twice. A nightly check asserts that every txnId balances and that cached balances equal the sums. If write volume ever outgrew one database, I would shard by merchant and keep the balance invariant per shard.

deepDives.title: Webhooks and the outbox
deepDives.problem: Two directions of messaging can each lose or duplicate events. Inbound, the PSP sends webhooks at least once, possibly out of order. Outbound, we must tell the order and payout services about state changes without telling them about changes that later rolled back.

options.name: Process webhooks inline, publish after commit
options.how: Handle the webhook in the HTTP request; after the DB commit, publish to the bus.
cons: A crash between commit and publish loses the event
Slow handling makes the PSP time out and resend

options.name: Store then process inbound; outbox outbound
options.how: Webhook receiver verifies the signature and inserts the raw event with a unique PSP event id, then returns 200. A processor applies events through the state machine. State changes write an outbox row in the same transaction; a relay publishes it and marks it sent.
pros: Duplicates are dropped by the unique id
Out-of-order events are handled by state rules
cons: Consumers still see duplicates from the relay and must dedupe
Adds a few seconds of delay

deepDives.choice: Use store-then-process plus an outbox. The state machine only allows forward moves (an 'authorized' webhook arriving after 'captured' is ignored and logged). The relay is at-least-once, so every consumer dedupes by event id. If I could not rely on webhooks arriving at all, I would add a poller that queries the PSP for any payment that stays in an in-between state for over 5 minutes.

diagram.title: Inbound webhook and outbound event
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as PSP
  participant W as Webhook receiver
  participant D as Database
  participant X as Processor
  participant R as Outbox relay
  participant B as Event bus
  P->>W: event E, signed
  W->>W: verify signature
  W->>D: insert E, unique event id
  W-->>P: 200
  X->>D: apply E, ledger lines, outbox row
  R->>D: read unsent outbox rows
  R->>B: publish PaymentCaptured
  R->>D: mark sent

deepDives.title: Reconciliation
deepDives.problem: Idempotency and the outbox cover the failures we thought of. Reconciliation catches the ones we did not: a bug, a manual change at the PSP, a webhook that never came. At $400 M/day, a 0.01% gap is $40 k/day.

options.name: Manual spot checks
options.how: Finance compares totals in a spreadsheet each month.
cons: Finds problems weeks late
Totals can match while individual payments are wrong

options.name: Automated line-by-line match
options.how: Load the PSP's daily settlement file (about 10 M lines). Join it to our captures and refunds by pspRef. Classify each line: matched, missing on our side, missing on theirs, amount differs. Auto-fix known patterns; open cases for the rest.
pros: Catches individual errors within a day
cons: Timing differences (a payment near midnight) create false alarms
Each PSP's file format needs its own parser

deepDives.choice: Run the automated line-by-line match daily, with a 2-day window for timing differences before raising a case. 'Missing on our side' usually means a lost webhook, and the fix is to replay that event through the normal processor, not to edit the ledger. If the case queue stays above a few hundred per day, that is a signal to fix the root cause in the payment flow, not to hire more reviewers.

deepDives.title: Why 'exactly once' really means effectively once
deepDives.problem: Across a network, a sender can never know whether a message that timed out was received. So delivery is always at most once (may lose) or at least once (may repeat). Interviewers want to hear how we still get exactly one charge.

options.name: Try for exactly-once delivery
options.how: Use transactional messaging features to deliver each message once.
pros: Works inside one system, such as one Kafka cluster with transactional producers and consumers
cons: Does not extend to an external PSP or to HTTP callers
Gives false confidence

options.name: At-least-once delivery plus idempotent effects
options.how: Retry until acknowledged; make every effect keyed so that applying it again changes nothing: unique keys on payments, attempts, ledger sourceRef and inbound event ids.
pros: Each key can be tested on its own
cons: Every new effect needs a key designed for it
Keys must be kept for at least as long as retries can happen

deepDives.choice: Design for at-least-once delivery plus idempotent effects. The outcome the business sees is one charge and one set of ledger lines, which is what people mean by exactly once. I would say this out loud in the interview and then list where each key lives. Reconciliation is the backstop that proves it worked.

failures: Circuit breaker opens; new payments fail fast with a clear message or route to a second PSP if configured; unknown attempts are resolved by the recovery worker once the PSP returns.
Our service crashes after the PSP charged but before we saved the result
The attempt row was saved as sent before the call; the recovery worker retries with the same key and gets the original result.
Webhook endpoint is slow and the PSP resends
Unique event id drops duplicates; receiver only stores and returns 200, keeping response time well under the PSP's timeout.
Payments still commit; orders confirm late; alert when the oldest unsent row is over 1 minute old; relay resumes from the last sent id.
Settlement file shows a capture we never recorded
Reconciler opens a case and replays the PSP's event for that payment through the normal processor; never patch the ledger by hand.
A bug posts unbalanced ledger lines
A database trigger or check per txnId rejects the commit; the nightly balance check catches anything that slipped through.
scale: 10× (100 M payments/day): about 46,000 ledger inserts/s at peak; shard payments and ledger by merchantId so each payment's state and lines stay on one shard.
Several PSPs: add a routing layer by card type, country and cost; reconciliation and idempotency are per provider; a payment's attempts can span providers but each attempt names one.
Multi-region: keep each merchant's money in one home region; read-only views elsewhere; avoid active-active writes on balances.

followups.q: How long do you keep idempotency keys?
answer: At least as long as clients can retry: 24 hours for our API is common.
PSP-side keys follow the PSP's window, often a day or more; after it, use the lookup fallback.
Unique keys on ledger sourceRef and event ids are kept forever, because they are part of the record.
A daily payout job reads each seller's ledger balance minus holds for disputes.
It writes a payout ledger transaction and an outbox event in one commit, then calls the bank or PSP payout API with the payout id as the key.
The payout's own settlement is reconciled like any other movement.

followups.q: How do you handle currency conversion?
answer: Store the original currency and amount; never mix currencies in one account.
Record conversions as their own ledger transaction through an FX account, with the rate used.
Reconcile in the currency the PSP settles in.
Use the PSP's sandbox plus a fake PSP that can time out, double-send webhooks and reorder them.
Property tests that random sequences of retries and crashes never produce more than one charge or unbalanced books.
Run reconciliation in staging daily against the sandbox's report.

followups.q: Why not let the order service call the PSP directly?
answer: Then every team re-implements keys, state and ledger rules, and gets them slightly wrong.
One payment service gives one ledger and one place to reconcile.
It also keeps the PSP credentials in one place.

mistakes: Storing amounts as floating point numbers.
Retrying a PSP call after a timeout without an idempotency key.
Keeping only a balance column and updating it, with no ledger lines.
Processing webhooks synchronously and assuming they arrive once and in order.
Claiming Kafka or a queue gives exactly-once end to end, including the PSP.

mid: Used a PSP and card tokens so raw card numbers never reach our servers
Required an Idempotency-Key on payment, capture and refund endpoints
Stored money as integer minor units with a currency code
Drew a payment state machine with at least created, authorized, captured and failed
senior: Saved an attempt record before calling the PSP and reused its id as the PSP's idempotency key
Wrote a balanced double-entry example with real amounts
Used an outbox for outgoing events and a unique event id for incoming webhooks
Explained the 'unknown' outcome after a timeout and how it gets resolved
Described daily line-by-line reconciliation and how mismatches are fixed
staff: Explained why exactly-once delivery is impossible across the PSP boundary and how idempotent effects give the same result
Chose merchantId as the shard key and kept a payment's state and ledger lines together
Planned PSP outages: circuit breaking, second provider, recovery of unknown attempts
Defined how corrections are made (reversing entries only) and who can trigger them
